title: Online disputes: Faster processing may not improve justice
desc: Contrasts participation gains with representation gaps, uninformed concessions and unresolved standards for AI assistance and adjudication.

kps.k: The central dispute is whether online dispute resolution expands meaningful access to justice or merely processes unrepresented people’s cases more efficiently.
kps.d: The sources distinguish easier participation from fair, accurate and enforceable outcomes. Within Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice, Prescott argues that reducing defaults and access costs strengthens substantive law, while Spaulding questions whether early, interest-based settlements reflect legal rights and defenses. The consumer-claims article likewise argues that digitisation should improve justice rather than simply reproduce existing procedures online. These positions concern institutional design and measures of success, not a simple division between support for and opposition to technology.

qs.q: While the deﬁning virtue of ODR technology to                date is its capacity to improve the accessibility of courts for litigants, the phrase                “access to justice” hinges on what it means to achieve justice,7 and any useful access-                to-justice criterion must ask whether laws and institutions resolve disputes appropri-                ately – that is, accurately and fairly.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: ODR can and should be able to surpass traditional offline processes in helping people deal with everyday legal problems in a fair, timely, and accessible manner.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Existing evidence supports participation and operational gains more clearly than improved substantive outcomes.
kps.d: McCormack reports that a six-court Michigan ticket-review study found 80 percent less staff time and average resolution in two rather than seven weeks; 39 percent of users said they could not have attended in person. Prescott qualifies reported improvements as comparisons with other unrepresented litigants. Adoption reports establish diffusion, not effectiveness: Engstrom describes roughly 200 jurisdictions implementing or piloting ODR after COVID-era expansion, while Pew presents faster debt-case resolution as an implementation goal and announces evaluations rather than completed findings. These results do not establish GenAI effectiveness.

qs.q: According to a study of outcomes in six                Michigan courts, this online ticket-review system reduces court staff time by 80                percent, and cases are resolved in an average of two weeks instead of seven.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: advances are relative to a pro se baseline where the relevant control groups of            litigants are also unrepresented.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Simplified procedures leave a representation gap and may expose weaker parties to uninformed concessions.
kps.d: Prescott argues that legal expertise and outcome assessment remain valuable online and predicts persistent or larger representation disparities. The consumer-claims article warns that informal procedures can conceal the legal knowledge needed to succeed; information alone cannot ensure enforcement. Pew’s debt-court report finds largely one-sided outcomes and relays Lisa Stifler’s warning that consumers may unknowingly waive rights or defenses. Spaulding argues that settlement-oriented platforms can strengthen creditors or the state against unrepresented individuals, while acknowledging benefits between similarly situated parties. His cited 2010 FTC evidence on complex debt defenses also challenges the assumption that low monetary value means low complexity or low stakes.

kps.k: Proposed AI assistance targets unmet need, but decision support, automated adjudication and lawyer displacement remain distinct claims.
kps.d: Prescott proposes approximating selected lawyer functions through outcome information, options guidance and reduced identity or professional-status signaling; he expressly rejects a claim of lawyer obsolescence. The consumer-claims article prioritises personalised assistance before negotiation or adjudication, with possible translation, evidence organisation and procedural guidance. It treats these GenAI functions as conditional proposals, not demonstrated capabilities. Can Robots Be Lawyers? estimates minimal employment effects at the time of writing because existing systems mainly served disputes that could not economically support a lawyer. The European Ethical Charter separately urges evaluators to identify whether a system actually uses machine learning, expert rules or basic automation, and whether it guides or prescribes outcomes.

qs.q: In what follows, I identify three speciﬁc beneﬁts of legal representation – outcome            prediction, options guidance, and obfuscation/translation – and I argue that they can            be approximated through court technology.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: The disputes that these systems  resolve are generally small stakes e-commerce issues, for which it would not be economically  feasible to hire a lawyer and litigate (such that lawyer labor is not being replaced).101 Similarly,  expert systems are generally directed at reaching new markets rather than improving efficiency  in existing tasks).
qs.a: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law · Academia · 2017

kps.k: Disagreement over the proper comparison baseline shapes both accuracy standards and reform priorities.
kps.d: Prescott argues that critics compare ODR with idealised courts rather than actual systems marked by costs, bias and thin procedures. The consumer-claims authors similarly reject perfection as the threshold for assistance, noting human error and widespread absence of help, while calling for task-specific investigation of GenAI errors and comparison with alternative tools. Spaulding insists that doing better than no assistance is insufficient: procedural-fairness standards and alternatives such as funded counsel must also guide evaluation. Thus, the practical dispute concerns what evidence justifies deployment and which alternatives courts should fund, not whether hallucinations or existing court failures can be ignored.

qs.q: These tools do not need to be perfect – humans make errors and moreover, currently, many consumers receive no assistance at all.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

qs.q: 285                 evidence-based standard of safety and efﬁcacy, not the condition of the untreated,                ODR should be judged by comparison to standards of procedural fairness and the                costs of alternatives such as expanding access to counsel.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Client-centred safeguards translate broad access goals into concrete design requirements.
kps.d: Legal Aid in the United States: An Update for 2023 reports NLADA’s qualitative consultation with 53 participants through focus groups and interviews over 13 months. Participants identified distrust, security concerns and assistance needs while recognising ODR’s potential; these are consultation findings, not evidence of achieved benefits. NLADA recommends transparency, vulnerable-client-centred design, accessible routes out of ODR and proportionate data collection with equity evaluation. Spaulding adds informed opt-in, merits assessment, separation of negotiation from adjudication, recorded reasons and affordable appeals. The European Ethical Charter calls for clear access to a judge and warns against private services presenting themselves as courts.

qs.q: NLADA conducted this study over the course of 13 months, during which it held seven focus groups and a number of individual interviews.
qs.a: Legal Aid in the United States: An Update for 2023 · Academia · 2023

qs.q: If one speaks of a court, it must be the form of organisation defined by the European Convention on Human Rights and not simply a private justice institution with the mere appearance of state justice60.
qs.a: European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment · Regulators & courts · 2018

kps.k: Public accountability depends on who controls ODR, how it uses data and whether assistance becomes rights-affecting decision-making.
kps.d: Spaulding warns that proprietary code, undisclosed contracts, variable data practices and settlement-inducing fees can weaken accountability; his fee example includes a low-income waiver qualification. He also objects to surveillance-based preventive compliance and warns of vendor concentration, treating these outcomes as avoidable risks. Prescott responds that courts can build their own systems and design for public scrutiny and litigant voice. The consumer-claims article advocates continuing testing, monitoring and governance grounded in participation and due process. Certifying Legal AI Assistants tentatively interprets EU high-risk classification as distinguishing informational guidance from rights-affecting decisions; that remains the source’s qualified legal interpretation, not a categorical exemption for legal guidance.

qs.q: Contract terms between courts and private vendors of ODR software are not            generally available to the public.116 This makes any comparison with the costs of            alternatives to ODR such as civil Gideon117 difﬁcult to assess.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: As Richard Reuben has argued, these values in turn can be used in governance ‘to understand, assess, and constructively cultivate the democratic character of a dispute-resolution method, process, or system’.182 They may also be important in benchmarking operational standards on testing, monitoring and evaluation, which in turn are critical to maintaining accountability between the public, the system and the state.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Infrastructure and institutional capacity constrain expansion independently of model capability.
kps.d: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice identifies fragmented record ownership and incompatible court IT as barriers to reform. Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice presents the National Open Court Data Standards as a foundation for coordination, while stressing that the initiative collects and cleanses data rather than interpreting it or delivering interoperable AI. The consumer-claims article adds limited dispute-system design expertise and fragmented oversight under Australian federalism. These accounts imply that sustainable deployment requires data coordination, maintenance capacity and explicit governance alongside usable assistance; purchasing a model or expanding platform availability does not supply those foundations.

qs.q: As many have noted, inter-jurisdictional            differences are also severe, yielding an innovation-choking checkerboard of 14,000            federal, state, and local court jurisdictions with data and IT infrastructures that            cannot talk to one another.39 The pandemic has spurred important changes in            how courts deliver justice, but much work remains to be done.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

vlens.an: The curated academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction between faster or easier online participation and meaningful access to justice, while materially developing it into a broader framework for evaluation and design. Their common reasons are that operational measures such as speed, staff-time savings, reduced defaults and platform adoption do not establish accurate, fair or enforceable outcomes; unrepresented users may still lack legal knowledge, bargaining power and the capacity to recognise or assert rights; and AI assistance must be distinguished from settlement support, rights-affecting adjudication and lawyer displacement. The sources extend the proposition through concrete safeguards and institutional requirements, including vulnerable-client-centred design, accessible off-ramps, merits assessment, task-specific accuracy testing, transparency, public accountability and continuing governance. Material variation remains. The edited volume contains a genuine internal debate: Prescott emphasises gains relative to deficient existing courts and proposes technology that approximates selected lawyer functions, whereas Spaulding stresses representation asymmetries, uninformed concessions and procedural-fairness baselines. The consumer-claims article is conditionally optimistic about personalised GenAI assistance but treats its benefits as unproven. The employment study redirects part of the analysis toward the difference between theoretical substitution and limited contemporary displacement. One source redirects more substantially toward data interoperability and court capacity as prerequisites, while two bibliographic excerpts provide too little substantive evidence to determine a position. These sources are a curated selection and should not be treated as representative of academic opinion generally.

qs.q: GenAI may advance or threaten these goals, but there is likely no technological ‘quick fix’ to the complex problem of access to justice in small claims disputes involving under-resourced and relatively inexperienced parties such as consumers.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: This access-to-justice and civil-society source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that faster or more accessible online processing does not by itself establish improved justice. It recognises concrete participation and administrative promise: ODR can let people respond remotely, reduce resolution time and help courts manage caseloads. But it treats those benefits mainly as aims or potential gains rather than demonstrated improvements in fair or accurate outcomes. Its central qualification is substantive: consumers—especially unrepresented debt defendants—may unknowingly waive rights, claims or defences, so implementation requires consumer safeguards, recognised best practices and evaluation of risks and benefits. The source therefore reflects a consistent but internally qualified position: favourable toward usable online assistance and easier court participation, while rejecting speed, adoption or availability as sufficient measures of justice. As this is one curated source, its position should not be read as representative of all access-to-justice or civil-society perspectives.

qs.q: Since early 2019, chief justices of the supreme courts in Hawaii, Iowa, Texas, and Utah have highlighted ODR as a key priority in their State of the Judiciary addresses.107  Some jurisdictions—such as West Valley City, Utah, and Franklin County, Ohio—have begun using ODR for small debt claims in part to reduce the time that cases take to resolve.108 However, moving debt collection cases online is not a panacea.
qs.a: How Debt Collectors Are Transforming the Business of State Courts · Access to justice · 2020

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional-body sources support the proposition that faster or more widely available online dispute resolution does not by itself establish improved justice. The European Ethical Charter provides the clearest position: anticipated access-to-justice gains are presented as advocates’ expectations, while actual benefits, the technology’s contribution and its integration into judicial procedure require case-specific assessment. It also emphasises transparency, neutrality, institutional legitimacy and clear recourse to a judge. There is material internal variation in evidentiary strength rather than direction: The Landscape of Civil Litigation in State Courts documents the diffusion of ODR but supplies no evidence about fairness, representation, accuracy or substantive outcomes, so its position is independently unclear. This limited selection should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: The potential benefits of an ODR system, its degree of integration into a complete judicial process (from pre-litigation to actual litigation) and the almost decisive role of AI in the execution of the process must therefore be properly assessed on a case-by-case basis.
qs.a: European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment · Regulators & courts · 2018

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources support the proposition that online dispute resolution may improve participation, speed and court administration without thereby demonstrating fairer substantive outcomes. Their common reasoning is that diffusion and operational efficiency are not evidence of justice gains: meaningful access also depends on usable assistance, informed participation, protection of rights and defences, transparency, and continued judicial recourse. Material variation lies in emphasis. The debt-court report focuses on one-sided collection proceedings and the danger of consumers unknowingly conceding rights; the European Ethical Charter develops case-specific assessment and institutional safeguards; and the civil-litigation landscape source establishes ODR’s availability but provides too little outcome evidence to take a clear position. The automation scholarship extends the discussion by distinguishing theoretical replacement of lawyers or judges from actual labour-market displacement, estimated as minimal at the time because ODR mainly handled matters that could not economically support counsel. That extension is compatible with, but not necessary to, the period’s overall support for the proposition. Because these are curated sources, this synthesis describes their relationship to the proposition and does not indicate the prevalence of these views among authors or institutions in the period.

qs.q: The potential benefits of an ODR system, its degree of integration into a complete judicial process (from pre-litigation to actual litigation) and the almost decisive role of AI in the execution of the process must therefore be properly assessed on a case-by-case basis.
qs.a: European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment · Regulators & courts · 2018

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources accept the proposition’s central distinction between faster online processing and meaningful access to justice, while materially developing it through design and governance requirements. They report clearer evidence of reduced participation barriers, staff time and resolution time than of fairer or more legally accurate outcomes. Common concerns are that unrepresented parties may remain disadvantaged, settlement-oriented systems may obscure rights and defenses, and operational efficiency may be mistaken for substantive justice. The sources therefore add concrete safeguards: vulnerable-client-centred design, transparency, accessible off-ramps, equity evaluation, merits assessment, privacy protection, affordable review and public accountability. They also sharpen the regulatory distinction between systems that provide information or promote settlement and systems that make rights-affecting decisions. Material variation remains: Prescott argues that well-designed court technology can approximate selected lawyer functions and should be compared with the serious shortcomings of existing courts, whereas Spaulding stresses representation gaps, repeat-player advantages and procedural-fairness baselines, including funded counsel. The legal-aid source is cautiously constructive but questions whether ODR expansion is driven by low-income clients’ needs; the EU-focused source contributes a qualified classification argument rather than outcome evidence; and the bibliographic excerpt is too thin to establish a position. These sources are curated examples, so their alignment should not be treated as representative of all writing from the period. Much of the evidence also concerns ODR generally rather than demonstrated GenAI performance.

qs.q: While the deﬁning virtue of ODR technology to                date is its capacity to improve the accessibility of courts for litigants, the phrase                “access to justice” hinges on what it means to achieve justice,7 and any useful access-                to-justice criterion must ask whether laws and institutions resolve disputes appropri-                ately – that is, accurately and fairly.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Those are:          Be Transparent          Make it (Vulnerable) Client-Centered          Create Multiple and Easy to Use Off-Ramps          Get Good Data, But Not Too Much, and Evaluate for Equity                                  DELIVERY RESEARCH
qs.a: Legal Aid in the United States: An Update for 2023 · Academia · 2023

elens.an: The 2025 material builds on the proposition that faster online processing is not, by itself, meaningful access to justice. It materially develops that claim by identifying two sets of prerequisites for adoption at scale. The consumer-disputes source specifies substantive and institutional safeguards: support for users’ legal and digital capability, personalised early assistance, task-specific investigation of GenAI accuracy, and continuing governance grounded in fairness, due process and public legitimacy. It treats GenAI’s benefits as conditional proposals rather than demonstrated improvements in outcomes. The interoperability source supplies a complementary but differently framed contribution: it concentrates on standardised court data, coordination and local implementation capacity rather than directly assessing whether ODR produces fair or enforceable outcomes. Thus, the principal internal variation is between a justice-and-governance account of responsible ODR design and an infrastructure-first account of scalable legal AI. Neither source establishes that adoption at scale has improved substantive justice, and the latter largely redirects attention from that outcome question to the foundations needed for deployment.

qs.q: GenAI may advance or threaten these goals, but there is likely no technological ‘quick fix’ to the complex problem of access to justice in small claims disputes involving under-resourced and relatively inexperienced parties such as consumers.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

elens.an: For the current wave (2026), the sole supplied source record neither supports nor challenges the proposition that faster online dispute processing may fail to improve substantive justice. The excerpt consists only of bibliographic references concerning topics such as online dispute resolution, nonlawyer advice, regulation and access to justice. Without substantive claims, evidence, reasoning, predictions or recommendations from the author, it is not possible to determine the source’s view on participation gains, representation gaps, uninformed concessions, AI assistance, adjudication standards or safeguards. The cited titles cannot be treated as evidence of the author’s position, so no common rationale or internal variation can be established for this curated time-period evidence.
